Hexapod Mk1: Engineering Design Notebook

Project with Oli. The real hexapod behind the Robot Sim digital twin.

This notebook records the end-to-end design process in order: requirements, concepts, analysis, decisions, verification and open questions. It is compiled from the dated entries in docs/notebook/entries/. The tables marked (generated) are rebuilt from the current CAD outputs every time the notebook is compiled, so they always match the files in the repo.

Compile it:

python robot-sim/docs/notebook/build_notebook.py

This writes robot-sim/docs/notebook/Hexapod_Mk1_Design_Notebook.html, a single file with every image embedded. Print it to PDF from a browser if you need a PDF.

To refresh the CAD snapshots first, run save_snapshots(<folder>) from the generator inside Fusion (see entry 11).

Revisions.

  • Rev A: entries 01–04.
  • Rev B (bus servos, rechargeable power, real vendor CAD, harness): entries 05–12.
  • Rev B2 (leg study, onboard control and sensors, radio, brain module, full wiring, MuJoCo): entries 13–17.
  • Open items: entry 18.
  • Rev B2 RC build (remote control first, budget femurs; the autonomy build kept as the upgrade): entry 20. All versions: VERSIONS.md.
  • Hexapod Mini (a separate, remote-control-only robot for under $200, in robot-sim/mini/): entry 19.

01 · Requirements and constraints

2026-11-25

Goal. A real six-legged robot that Oli can print, build and drive from the Robot Sim. The robot and the sim share hexapod.config.js, so the CAD must match it, or the config must change with it.

Fixed inputs from the simulator.

  • Leg 45 / 75 / 120 mm (coxa / femur / tibia).
  • Six coxa mounts at front ±60, +110; middle ±80, 0; rear ±60, −110 mm.
  • Splay 35°.
  • Body about 260 × 140 mm.

Requirements, in the user's priority order.

  1. Printability (DFM).
  2. Every part fits a 220 × 220 × 250 mm bed (note anything that needs 180 mm).
  3. Flat print faces, 45° overhang rule, teardrop holes.
  4. PLA/PETG walls, 0.2–0.3 mm fits, M3 heat-set inserts.
  5. Assembly (DFA).
  6. Few unique parts: identical legs, mirrored only if unavoidable.
  7. One fastener type.
  8. Servos drop in from one direction.
  9. Captive inserts, support on both sides of every joint, self-locating features.
  10. Fillets and chamfers on stress corners, and an elephant-foot chamfer on first-layer edges.
  11. Room for the electronics, including a battery you can swap without taking the robot apart.
  12. A modular top deck: grid, quick-release, connector, example adapter, front sensor bracket.

Added later (rev B, entry 05).

  • A rechargeable battery that powers everything.
  • Actuators that are easy to buy and strong enough (at least 2× their rated torque).
  • The manufacturers' real CAD for every standard part.
  • Fillets and chamfers wherever stress needs them, with no interference.
  • Every wire, cable and connection modelled.
  • This notebook.

Safety and tone. Weapon attachments stay toys: an IR/LED "laser" and a foam-ball launcher. LiPo handling follows hobby safety practice for a student.

02 · Concept: Mk1 rev A (MG996R + PCA9685)

2026-11-25

Architecture.

  • 18 × MG996R PWM servos on two PCA9685 boards, with an ESP32 bridging USB from the sim.
  • 2S LiPo through a UBEC.
  • Two 5 mm body plates 45 mm apart.
  • Coxa: a printed U-clevis around the coxa servo, plus a cradle for the femur servo.
  • Femur: a clevis plus a cradle for the tibia servo.
  • Tibia: a clevis and a tapered shank.
  • Every joint had a 623ZZ bearing on an M3 bolt opposite the servo horn.

Key decisions.

  • Plates grew 21 mm lobes round each coxa axis so the servo tab screws had material under them. The body became 262 × 202 mm.
  • The plates were split in two with T-shaped jigsaw keys, and the top and bottom seams were offset, so they fit a 220 mm bed.
  • The left legs reuse the right-leg parts, rotated (not mirrored).
  • The generator builds every part from primitives and adds fillets automatically: it detects concave edges with a two-point containment test.

03 · Rev A verification: interference and joint ranges

2026-11-25

Interference check. Fusion's interference analysis on the whole assembly found and fixed:

  • the adapter rail's root fillet rubbing the receiver slot;
  • a femur fillet under the tibia servo tab;
  • a bracket fillet dipping into the plate edge;
  • the servo horn overlapping its spline;
  • a battery tray fillet touching the battery.

Joint sweep. Each joint was driven to its extremes. Rev A was limited by:

  • femur down ≤ 35°: the femur cradle hits the coxa cradle;
  • tibia fold-in ≤ 45°.

The simulation session then measured the gait's real commanded ranges. The sim asked for a −148° tibia fold, so the sim capped its gait at −135°.

Lesson carried into rev B. Joint limits and gait ranges must be checked together. A fold limit becomes a minimum reach in the inverse kinematics (IK), the maths that turns a foot position into joint angles.

04 · Rev A load check: the problem

2026-11-25

CAD massabout 2.7 kg
Load casetripod stance (three feet down), foot 85 mm out from the femur axis
Femur torque needed7.7 kg·cm
MG996R (6 V)11 kg·cm stall, about 3.5 kg·cm continuous
Femur load70 % of stall, far beyond continuous duty

The gait's widest stance made it worse: feet reached up to 160–190 mm from the femur axis during sprint plus turn.

Conclusion. Rev A would walk at a stand, but it would cook its femur servos with any attachment on. That, plus the request for a rechargeable power system and real vendor CAD, triggered rev B.

05 · Rev B brief

2026-11-25

  1. Actuators. Easy to buy, with official CAD, and at least 2× rated (continuous) torque in the worst case: tripod stance with the full robot plus a 0.4 kg attachment, at the widest stance the gait uses. Bus servos with feedback are a plus for the twin. Keep the USB protocol.
  2. Power. One rechargeable pack powers everything.
  3. Sized for ≥ 30 min walking, with an idle / walking / peak current budget.
  4. Charge port in the robot, and a battery you can still swap.
  5. Main switch, fuse, XT60, logic buck, current and voltage sensing, firmware low-voltage cutoff.
  6. Attachment port with switched rails and stated limits.
  7. Student-safe: no bare cells, fusing, strain relief.
  8. Real CAD. Manufacturer STEP models for the servos, boards and standard parts. Downloaded only from official sources, with licences respected.
  9. Redesign and re-check. Collision sweep, re-export everything, update the config, firmware and docs, save a new version to the cloud.

Later in the same session the user added:

  • fillets and chamfers on every stress corner, with no interference;
  • every wire, cable and connection modelled;
  • this design notebook.

06 · Actuator selection and load analysis

2026-11-25

Candidates (checked on the web on 2026-11-25):

Servo12 V stall / ratedPriceOfficial CADVerdict
Feetech STS3215 / Waveshare ST321530 / 10 kg·cmabout $20–22Waveshare STEPChosen for the coxa and tibia
Feetech STS325050 / 16 kg·cmabout $97–99Same housing as the ST3215Chosen for the femur
Hiwonder HTS-35H35 kg·cm at 11.1 V, rated not publishedabout $30None foundRejected: no rated torque, no CAD
DS3218MG (PWM)20 kg·cm stallabout $15–19None officialRejected: PWM, no feedback

Load model (cad/load_calc.py).

  • Femur: F × the horizontal distance from the femur axis to the foot.
  • Tibia: the worst F × knee-to-foot offset over the stance ring.
  • Coxa: a sideways push of 0.3 F.
  • Here F = (m_robot + 0.4 kg) · g / 3.

The gait-reach study showed that the uncapped sim gait can ask for 194 mm from the coxa axis. That needs 16 kg·cm at the femur, and nothing affordable carries that at a 2× margin. Decision: keep every stance foot 80–115 mm from its coxa axis (footReachMin/Max, nominal 100 mm).

07 · Power system

2026-11-25

Voltage. The STS servos run at 12 V nominal, so the pack is 3S (12.6 V full, 9.9 V cut-off).

Chemistry and pack.

  • 3S1P 21700 Li-ion packs (Molicel P45B, 4.5 Ah, 45 A): the commercial packs found are triangular bundles about 50 mm tall, which don't fit between plates set 30.4 mm apart by the servo case. Building a pack means spot-welding bare cells, which isn't suitable for a student project. Rejected.
  • Gens Ace 3S 4000 mAh 50–60C hard-case LiPo: 138.5 × 43 × 24.5 mm, about 305 g, XT60, sold everywhere. Chosen. It slides in from the rear between the rear coxa servos.

Protection. Battery-side protection is a balance charger (which does CC/CV and per-cell balancing), plus:

  • a 20 A ATC fuse right after the XT60;
  • a Pololu MOSFET switch with reverse-polarity protection;
  • an ACS724 ±30 A current sensor and a voltage divider read by the ESP32;
  • a firmware cut-off at 3.4 V/cell (3 s debounce).

A separate BMS was considered. Cheap 3S boards limit current and add a failure point, and the balance charger plus fuse plus cut-off covers each risk a BMS would.

Charge port. The rear panel carries the pack's XT60 charge leads and a JST-XH 4 balance extension. Charge with the robot off, attended, on a non-flammable surface; a bag charge out of the robot is always the option.

Current budget.

StateCurrent
Logicabout 0.2 A
Standingabout 2 A
Walking4–6 A
Peakabout 25 A transient
Theoretical stall50 A

Runtime. 3.2 Ah usable gives 32–48 min walking.

08 · Manufacturer CAD and licensing

2026-11-25

Downloaded from official servers, with no login and no executables (cad/vendor/fetch_vendor_cad.py):

  • Waveshare ST3215 STEP and 2D drawing.
  • Waveshare Servo Driver with ESP32 STEP.
  • Pololu D36V28Fx, Big MOSFET switch and ACS724 STEPs.

Licences. None of these files states a redistribution licence, so the repo links to them and fetches them instead of committing copies. The generator copies them to a short temp path, because the repo path exceeds Windows' 260-character limit. It falls back to datasheet envelopes if they're missing. 09 · Rev B mechanical redesign

2026-11-25

The servo sandwich. Every servo is clamped between two 5 mm printed faces sitting on its real case faces, with pockets for the label boss and pad and 2 × M2 into the case on each side. As a result:

  • the plate gap is set by the servo (30.4 mm);
  • the body origin is the coxa-joint height;
  • the plates sit at +13.8…+18.8 and −21.6…−16.6 mm.

Two-sided joints. The STS servos have a driven horn on one side and an idler disc on the other, so every bracket bolts to both through pads. The joint is supported on both sides by the servo's own bearings, and the rev A 623 bearings were removed.

Links.

  • Coxa: CoxaMain (two horn arms, web, + clamp plate) and CoxaCap (− clamp plate). It's split because a one-piece U with both clamp plates can't print without supports.
  • Femur: two arms with bosses that clamp the tibia servo, and a bridge.
  • Tibia: its arms moved outboard of the femur arms. With both pairs in the same planes, the tibia could only fold 30°; outboard arms plus a chamfered bridge give 45°.

Body.

  • The plate edge sits 11.5 mm inside each coxa axis.
  • Integral pillars (no standoffs).
  • The battery bay was moved rearward to make room for a front power strip.
  • Everything now fits a 180 mm bed.

10 · Fillets, chamfers and interference

2026-11-25

Per the user's request, the generator now applies four finishes automatically, before any hole or pocket is cut:

  • 3 mm fillets on the main load-path inside corners;
  • 2 mm on every other inside corner (pad and boss roots, pillar roots);
  • 0.8 mm edge breaks on the outside edges of each part's top face;
  • 0.5 mm elephant-foot chamfers on bed-side edges.

Sliding fits stay sharp: the dovetail slot and the jigsaw keys.

Interference those fillets caused, and the fixes:

  • 1.5 mm rail-root fillets against the receiver lip: rail fillet reduced to 0.5 mm, inside the lip's 0.8 mm round.
  • Fillets inside the dovetail slot: that zone is excluded from the fillet pass.

11 · Wiring harness, modelled

2026-11-25

Every cable is a routed pipe of real diameter, and every connector a body, each in the rigid group it moves with.

Iteration history.

  1. First routing. Many crossings in the cramped front bay. The power chain was simplified: the ACS724 moved directly under the MOSFET switch, and the attachment port lost its 5 V line (attachments make their own).
  2. Joint sweeps with the cables. Leg cables drawn rigid in one link were hit by the moving parts. Leads were split where they cross a joint, at a point on the joint axis, so neither segment moves as the joint turns.
  3. Still hit at tibia fold and femur-down. Leads running under the femur were in the way. A 3-socket bus hub on top of each coxa fixed it: one lead to the femur servo, and one over the femur arms to the tibia servo's top socket.
  4. Final sweep. Clean at every pose inside the limits. The femur-down limit was tightened to 10° (the gait needs 4°), and the tibia fold is coupled with the femur angle (−135° when the femur is level or up, −132° when it is up to 10° down).

12 · Firmware and protocol

2026-11-25

  • Board. Waveshare Servo Driver with ESP32. Servo bus on GPIO18/19 at 1 Mbaud (pins confirmed from Waveshare's example source).
  • Library. Feetech SCServo (SMS_STS).
  • IDs. Leg L, joint J → ID 1 + 3L + J. Attachment servos are IDs 21–25.

Protocol unchanged. The sim still sends S,<deg>… at 25 Hz. The firmware converts 0–180° to 4096-step positions (2048 = centre) and sends one SyncWritePosEx per frame.

New telemetry. B,<mV>,<mA>,<°C>,<state> at 2 Hz.

Safety logic.

  • 0.5 s link timeout → all servos relax.
  • Soft-start speed for 2 s after a relink.
  • Low-voltage cut-off at 10.2 V (3 s debounce), recovering above 11.0 V.

13 · Leg architecture study (rev B2)

2026-11-25

Question (Oli and the parent brief). Could smarter kinematics (linkages, coupled legs, fewer actuators) do the job with less? Oli then added a hard rule: the body must still tilt, and ideally change height.

Options studied (full table and sources in KINEMATICS.md):

  • 3-DOF serial, 18 servos;
  • 3-DOF with the knee servo moved to the hip through a four-bar;
  • 2-DOF pantograph, 12 servos;
  • hybrid, 16 servos;
  • coupled tripods, 2–4 motors;
  • Jansen / Klann, 2 motors;
  • RHex, 6 motors.

Decision: keep the 3-DOF serial leg.

  1. Excluded by the tilt rule. Coupled, linkage-walker and RHex designs can't control each foot's height, so they can't tilt the body.
  2. The four-bar knee is too small a gain. It saves only about 6 % femur torque, because rev B already points the tibia servo's case back towards the femur axis. And four-bar knees reach under about 90°, where Mk1 needs 165°.
  3. The 2-DOF pantograph gives up too much. It saves 6 servos (≈ $130) but costs:
  4. about 2 mm of foot slip per step;
  5. no strafing;
  6. no stance-width control (our load cap);
  7. about 72 pivots.

For the simulator. Nothing changes: 3 DOF, the same lengths and limits, no passive joints.

14 · Control system on the robot

2026-11-25

Brief. Balance, walking, tilting, climbing up and down uneven ground, with every sensor and controller on the robot itself.

Controller. The rev B Waveshare board has too few free pins (one), so the main controller became an Adafruit Feather ESP32-S3. The Waveshare board stays as a servo-bus bridge that also reads the battery.

Sensors.

  • BNO085 IMU under the belly, on grommets.
  • Omron D2F micro-switch in every tibia tip, sealed by a sliding TPU boot with a plunger nub.
  • VL53L1X looking 30° down from the front bracket.
  • Bus-servo readback of position, temperature and load.

Control layers (all equations in CONTROL.md):

  • the servos' internal PID, softened for terrain;
  • IK identical to the simulator, plus a lift cap near the body;
  • a tripod / ripple / wave gait with the stance-window rule (feet 80–115 mm);
  • body pose;
  • IMU balance (PI on attitude, D on the gyro);
  • a stability margin that switches tripod → ripple below 25 mm;
  • touchdown search and terrain following;
  • safety: kill, low battery, tip, temperature, link loss.

Verification (host tests on the PC, firmware/test):

CheckResult
IK ↔ FKRound trip matches
StandingAll feet on the ground
WalkingThe two tripods are never up together
Sprint + turnFeet stay 86–115 mm out
Ripple / waveAt least 4 / 5 feet down
Tripod margin83 mm
12° slopeLevelled to 0.05° in 4 s
CRSFFrames round-trip; a bad CRC is rejected

What the tests changed.

  1. They found that a sprinting swing foot would need the tibia folded past its limit, which led to the lift cap.
  2. The first balance gains took 3 s to level; Ki went from 0.6 to 2.0.

Terrain limits from the geometry.

  • Step up 40 mm (terrain mode, 105 mm body height).
  • Step down 131.6 mm − body height (about 27 mm at the 105 mm terrain height). The sim found the femur's −10° limit sets this.
  • Full levelling about 10° (balance output clamped there).

Fixed after the sim review. Touchdown heights are now taken in the IMU's level frame, so the gait can't teach itself the body's tilt.

  • Slope 20° rated (static tipping at 29° in a tripod).

15 · Wiring every part

2026-11-25

Brief. Consider every wire from the battery to each load (including every motor), and put the wires in the assembly.

What changed from rev B.

  • Fusing. One 3 A PTC per leg branch on the side hubs, 5 A on J1, 1.1 A on the bridge, 1000 µF on each hub, and a star ground at the switch output.
  • Wire sizes. 14 AWG main path (0.26 V drop at a 25 A peak), 18 AWG hub trunks, 22 AWG servo leads (worst servo 3.5 % total drop), 28 AWG twisted foot leads.
  • New leads, all modelled:
  • six foot leads, each crossing the coxa, femur and knee axes on the axis;
  • the IMU lead from under the belly;
  • the bridge UART;
  • the Feather 5 V;
  • J1 AUX;
  • sonar and ToF;
  • the receiver and its antenna;
  • the five brain-module cables.
  • New routing features:
  • plate tie slots;
  • femur fins;
  • tibia grooves, with a cross slot and an internal channel;
  • pod entries, with spares.

Iterations driven by the collision sweep.

  1. The ToF wedge first went inside the bottom plate. It moved to the flange top.
  2. A lid boss sat in a foot lead's path. The bosses moved.
  3. Pod leads crossed. Each lead got its own hole.
  4. The IMU board hit an insert column. The board moved.
  5. The foot lead ran over a horn-screw head. The groove moved to x = 4.5 mm.
  6. The femur fins hit the folding tibia at full fold. They moved next to the femur axis.

Final sweep. 46 of 49 poses are clean. That is the same as rev B: the only hits are at the coupled-limit corner.

The current cable table is in entry 11 (generated). The cut list, pin maps and assembly order are in WIRING.md.

16 · Remote control and autonomy

2026-11-25

Radio. An EdgeTX radio (RadioMaster TX16S MK3) with ExpressLRS. Both are open source and the radio is Lua-scriptable; it beat a Bluetooth gamepad (no telemetry, short range) and a home-made ESP-NOW radio.

Robot side.

  • An RP1 V2 receiver in the plastic pod, its antenna vertical on a lid post.
  • CRSF goes to the Feather.
  • Telemetry goes back to the radio: battery, attitude, mode, faults.
  • The Lua widget and the black-and-white script are in radio/.

Command priority. Safety > radio > brain (radio in auto, sticks centred) > USB host. Without a radio, the brain can't drive at all.

Brain module.

  • Compute. A Pi 5 instead of a Jetson Orin Nano: the OAK-D Lite runs the neural networks on its own VPU, and the Pi uses about 9 W against 15–25 W and costs about a third.
  • Packaging. A swappable top-deck module: Pi 5, OAK-D Lite, LD19 and a 5.5 A buck. It is 300 g, inside the 0.4 kg attachment allowance, and runs from J1. The Pi talks to the ESP32 over J1's two AUX lines; the Feather tells a brain from a weapon by AUX2's idle level.

ROS 2 Jazzy design.

  • slam_toolbox;
  • Nav2 (MPPI, omnidirectional);
  • elevation map;
  • OAK-D detections;
  • a battle behaviour tree;
  • an ONNX policy that sends R, residuals.

Details are in AUTONOMY.md.

17 · MuJoCo model and sim2real

2026-11-25

Oli picked MuJoCo.

The model. autonomy/mujoco/make_mjcf.py generates the MJCF (and a URDF) from the CAD build report and meshes:

  • masses per link;
  • the battery at its real position;
  • a payload body at the top mount;
  • STS servo position actuators with stall-torque limits;
  • the IMU and foot-touch sensors.

Its joint angles are the simulator's.

Checks (test_stand.py, passes):

  • The model stands at 89 mm, tilt 0.02°, all six feet loaded, femurs 0.22 N·m.
  • The firmware's own tripod gait walks it 0.58 m in 4 s at a 0.15 m/s command.

Training setup.

  • Gymnasium env: the policy learns residuals on top of the classical gait, so a zero output is the firmware gait.
  • Domain randomisation: payload, mass, CoM, friction, servo kp, latency, backlash, terrain.
  • Stable-Baselines3 PPO on the CPU (Windows-friendly); MuJoCo Playground on a Linux GPU is the upgrade path.
  • ONNX export to the Pi.

The ESP32 clamps and expires residuals, so the classical controller stays the safety net.

Status. The model and env work. Training hasn't been run yet.

19 · Hexapod Mini: a remote-control hexapod for under $200

2026-11-26

Brief. Mk1 costs $900–1,900. Oli also wants a small robot that:

  • walks, turns and strafes from a hand-held remote;
  • runs on a rechargeable battery;
  • is safe to build;
  • costs under US$200 for everything: filament, battery, charger and remote included.

It is remote-control only, with no autonomy. Everything is in robot-sim/mini/; the Mk1 files are unchanged.

Decisions

QuestionOptions looked atChosenWhy
ActuatorsMG90S, SG90, Feetech SCS0009 bus servos18 × MG90S ($43)The bus servos alone would cost $110–160. SG90 plastic gears strip
RemoteExpressLRS radio + receiver ($70–100), Bluetooth gamepadBluepad32 gamepad ($21, 8BitDo Lite 2)A fifth of the price, and it uses the ESP32's radio. A classic ESP32 is needed for Bluetooth Classic pads
Battery2S LiPo, 2S 186502 × 18650 (Molicel P28A) + 2S BMS + 10 A fuseSteel cans, charged outside the robot in a $7 charger, cell by cell
Servo powerone big buck, two small2 × Mini560 5 V 5 AFits under the deck, one per side

Total: about $196 with shipping. See BOM.md for the links, and for which prices were checked and which are approx.

Engineering

Conventions. The design follows Mk1's:

  • a parametric Fusion generator made from TemporaryBRep primitives;
  • inside-corner fillets, bed chamfers and edge breaks;
  • teardrop holes;
  • joints and rigid groups;
  • every wire modelled.

Leg. Coxa 30, femur 44, tibia 60 mm. Each joint has a horn arm, plus an idler arm on an M3 pin on the far side of the servo, so no joint hangs on a micro servo's shaft alone.

Parts. The six legs use the same three printed parts, turned rather than mirrored.

Load check. The weight is shared over a real tripod, not m g / 3:

  • the lone middle foot carries 44 % of the weight;
  • with the stance-window rule (middle feet within 61 mm of the coxa axis), the femur has 2.0–2.1 × the MG90S datasheet torque at 5 V;
  • the coxa and tibia have 3–5 ×.

The datasheet figure is a stall torque, which the design doc says plainly: the servos are worked hard, so the firmware sits the robot down whenever it is idle.

Interference. Fusion's interference analysis checks:

  • the neutral pose;
  • 20 poses per leg (coxa ±40°, femur and tibia past their limits);
  • neighbouring legs swung towards each other to the 25° firmware coxa limit.

The sweep found five problems, all fixed:

  • servo tabs in the tray wall;
  • an over-reaching sweep cut-out;
  • the tibia arm against the femur skin;
  • neighbouring legs at 40°;
  • fillets touching servos.

The final build is clean (see DESIGN.md §5).

Firmware. The ESP32 runs the IK and gait in the simulator's own conventions:

  • IK and tripod gait, with the stance-window rule;
  • Bluepad32 sticks;
  • arm/sit with A/B;
  • failsafes on pad loss and low battery, with the OE pin forcing the servos limp;
  • the sim's USB S, protocol.

Host tests pass. They cover the IK round trip, the tibia limit, that both tripods are never up, the stance window, the coxa range, coming to rest, and the channel map.

Not yet verified

  • Nothing has been printed, built or flashed.
  • The MG90S and board shapes are datasheet envelopes. Print the coxa fit test first.
  • The mass is a CAD estimate.
  • The servo directions are checked on the stand.

20 · Mk1 RC build: remote control first, autonomy later

2026-11-26

Question. Is the robot much cheaper if it is only driven by the radio and never runs on its own? Yes, so that's now the default build. The autonomous design stays in the repo as an upgrade.

Cost options considered

BuildWhat changesAll-in cost
Full autonomy (rev B2 as designed)STS3250 femurs + brain module + TX16S≈ US$1,920
RC onlyDrop the brain module≈ US$1,560
RC only + budget femurs (chosen)Also STS3215 femurs instead of STS3250≈ US$1,110
… with a RadioMaster PocketAlso the cheaper radio≈ US$950

Dropping the brain saves about $350. Dropping the six STS3250s saves about $460, the biggest single item.

What the budget femurs cost in margin

cad/load_calc.py: tripod stance, feet 80–115 mm from the coxa axis, 2.93 kg robot.

Top attachmentFemur requiredMargin vs rated (10 kg·cm)Margin vs stall (30 kg·cm)
0.4 kg (the autonomy allowance)7.77 kg·cm1.29×3.9×
0.2 kg (RC cap)7.22 kg·cm1.39×4.2×
STS3250 femurs, 0.4 kg (autonomy build)7.84 kg·cm2.04×6.4×

Decision.

  • The 2× target can't be met with STS3215 femurs at any useful payload. Instead, the RC build:
  • caps top attachments at 0.2 kg;
  • keeps the 80–115 mm stance window;
  • watches servo temperature in the B, telemetry and rests the robot above 60 °C.
  • 4.2× under stall means it stands and walks with room to spare. It will only run warm on long sessions.
  • The STS3250 drops into the same pocket, so the upgrade needs no reprinting.

What changed

  • Generator. cad/hexapod_mk1_fusion.py gained a BUILD = 'rc' | 'autonomy' switch:
  • it sets the femur servo model and its mass;
  • it shows the turret example on the top mount (RC) or the brain module (autonomy).
  • Files.
  • cad/Hexapod_Mk1.f3d and cad/build_report.json are now the RC build.
  • The autonomy build is kept as cad/Hexapod_Mk1_autonomy.f3d / build_report_autonomy.json.
  • The cloud document "Hexapod Mk1" (version 3) stays the autonomy build. The RC build is a new cloud document, "Hexapod Mk1 RC".
  • Docs.
  • DESIGN.md and BUILD.md describe both builds, with an RC load table.
  • ELECTRONICS.md marks the autonomy upgrade rows and totals both builds.
  • The simulator config uses build: 'rc', 2.93 kg.
  • MuJoCo now reads the autonomy report, since it exists for the brain's policy.
  • Versions. Every version, its git tag and its cloud document are listed in VERSIONS.md. The new tag is mk1-revB2-rc.

Verification

  • Cloud build. The RC build was rebuilt in Fusion with the vendor models; the renders in docs/img come from it.
  • Load check. Re-run for 2.93 kg + 0.2 kg (table above).
  • MuJoCo. Regenerated from the autonomy report: still stands at 88 mm and walks 0.58 m in 4 s.
  • Not yet done. Nothing has been built. The femur temperatures with STS3215s need measuring on the real robot.
